_: §5.1's divergence table, as data, listing only the rows Stage 1 touches.
The keys are the names the APPLICATIONS actually read — the environment
variables inside the containers, and the build arguments Vite inlines —
and NOT `.env.example`'s host-side names. That distinction is the whole
of H6: `.env.example` says OIDC_ISSUER_API and the compose file says
`API_ISSUER: ${OIDC_ISSUER_API}`, so the two files use different names
for one value. The host names are compose interpolation inputs; they are
not application configuration, and comparing them against Azure would
need a permanent alias table between two naming schemes — a list that
rots, which is the failure §19 warns about.
A row here with no key behind it fails, exactly as a key with no row
does. That is what stops the table decaying into a list of good
intentions.
CORRECTED AGAINST THE SHIPPED FILES (Task 26): the task brief's draft of
this file named API_OIDC_ISSUER, API_OIDC_AUDIENCE and the rest, which no
code reads — apps/api/src/config.ts reads API_ISSUER, API_AUDIENCE,
API_SUBJECT_CLAIM, API_GROUPS_CLAIM and API_REQUIRED_CLAIMS, with no
_OIDC_ infix. It also tabled the identity keys as divergences when their
NAMES are identical in both environments and only their VALUES differ,
which is the sameEverywhere kind.
CORRECTED AGAIN (C1): .env.example no longer has an OIDC_ISSUER_API. The
two names it used to carry, OIDC_ISSUER_API and OIDC_ISSUER_BROWSER, were
two names for what jose compares as ONE string, and the compose stack set
them to different values — so every token it minted was refused. There is
now one issuer (OIDC_ISSUER_BROWSER, fed to BOTH the browser's
VITE_OIDC_ISSUER and the API's API_ISSUER) and a separate
OIDC_DISCOVERY_API naming where the API fetches that issuer's keys. The
sentence above about host-side names being interpolation inputs is
unchanged and is why this file still tables API_DISCOVERY_URL, the name
the application reads, rather than OIDC_DISCOVERY_API.

rows.why: The API's and the browser's identity keys are the SAME NAMES in both environments and carry different values — Keycloak's issuer locally, Entra's in a tenant — so they are sameEverywhere, not a divergence. What genuinely exists in only one environment is Keycloak's own bootstrap and hostname: locally the issuer is a container this stack runs, and in a tenant it is somebody else's service. API_DISCOVERY_URL belongs to the same row and is the one key here that an APPLICATION reads. It exists locally because the local issuer has two addresses and only one of them is reachable from `api`: the browser obtains its token through the published port (localhost:8088), so that is the string stamped into `iss` and the string the API must demand, while discovery and JWKS have to be fetched over the container-network name. In Azure the two coincide — Entra is publicly reachable from the container — so apps/api/src/config.ts defaults it to API_ISSUER and the Azure template sets nothing. It is emphatically NOT an auth mode (S29/S30): it changes where keys are fetched, never which issuer is trusted or how a token is checked, and the same jwtVerify call with the same options runs in both environments.

The divergence lives INSIDE models.json — each entry's `credential.source` is `env`/`file` locally and `managed-identity`/`key-vault` in Azure — and models.json is mounted as a file in both environments under the same GATEWAY_MODELS_FILE key. GATEWAY_RECORDED_CREDENTIAL is the one application variable this row does carry, and it exists in ONE environment only, which is why it is a divergence rather than a sameEverywhere key: it is the credential the `recorded` provider names and never uses. `callModel`'s prepare() resolves a credential for every model before any adapter sees the request — one resolution path, no per-provider branch, because "this provider needs no key, so skip the resolver" is one edit away from "managed identity failed, so read the env var instead", which §10 forbids — so a recorded entry must still name a variable and that variable must be non-empty. Set by the compose file with a literal default, because the offline path is the one that is supposed to work with no keys at all; set by nothing in Azure, where there is no recorded provider to configure.

Local only, and deliberately so. In Azure every credential models.json declares resolves through the gateway's managed identity or Key Vault, so no provider key is an environment variable, a parameter or an output — which is the whole of S2's stronger property, expressed as an absence in infra/modules/containerApps.bicep.

Azurite cannot authenticate by managed identity (§5.1's own 'what local does not prove' list says so), so the two environments genuinely need different credential MATERIAL — and that is the whole of the divergence. API_BLOB_CREDENTIAL_SOURCE and API_BLOB_CONTAINER are now set in BOTH environments under identical names and moved to sameEverywhere when Task 24's infra/modules/storage.bicep and the api Container App's env block landed; the source key's VALUE selects which material is used, and resolveBlobCredential never falls back from one to the other (P14). What is left here is one key per environment, plus one that is easy to miss. The connection string exists only locally, and its material is the well-known, published, non-secret Azurite development credential; the account URL exists only in Azure. AZURE_CLIENT_ID is the one that is easy to miss and is tabled deliberately rather than treated as infrastructure noise: apps/api/src/blob/store.ts constructs `new DefaultAzureCredential()` with no options, and the managed-identity leg of that chain resolves a USER-ASSIGNED identity's client id from process.env.AZURE_CLIENT_ID and from nowhere else (@azure/identity 4.13.1, createDefaultManagedIdentityCredential — read in this repository's own node_modules). The api Container App has a user-assigned identity and no system-assigned one, so without this key every document byte read and write fails in Azure with every unit test green. It is read by a LIBRARY rather than by a configuration module, which is why it does not appear in the 'every key a config module reads is classified' check and why it needed tabling by hand. The absence of a connection-string OUTPUT in storage.bicep is S2's stronger property expressed as an absence, exactly as Stage 1 expressed it for provider keys — and it is more than a convention there: the account is created with shared-key authentication switched off, so an account key authenticates nothing even if one leaked.

GATEWAY_CALLER_AUTH itself is sameEverywhere — the key is set in both and its VALUE selects the mode — so what diverges is the material each mode needs: certificate paths and an allowed subject locally, a tenant, an audience and an allowed object id in Azure. GATEWAY_PUBLIC_ORIGIN joins them because it is the deployment's own public URL: Azure sets it from the web app's provisioned FQDN, and the compose stack has no provisioned FQDN to set it from. STAGE 4 TASK 17 ADDS THE WEBSOCKET HOP TO THIS ROW rather than a row of its own, because it is the same fact: what the ingress tier does to a request on its way in. Locally, infra/nginx/web.conf now carries a dedicated `location /api/v1/ws` with `proxy_http_version 1.1`, Upgrade/Connection headers and a 3600s read timeout -- proven through the published port in wsProxy.compose.test.ts, which is the one hop local development can exercise. In Azure the equivalent is the web Container App's `transport: 'auto'` ingress, which is what Container Apps documents for WebSockets and which is already set. It carries NO new environment key in either environment, which is why this row's key list is unchanged. THE INTERNAL HOP IS UNANSWERED: api's ingress is `transport: 'http'`, and whether an internal Container Apps ingress at http passes an Upgrade is not something the documentation settles or that any reachable environment could be asked. That is Spike 3's unanswered half and it is named as such in spike-3-report.md rather than guessed at.

rows.what: Which DNS resolves web's proxy upstream
rows.why: API_UPSTREAM is set in BOTH environments — it is sameEverywhere with different values, exactly like the identity keys in row 1 — because the SPA calls /api on its own origin in both and nginx forwards it. What exists in only one environment is the resolver: Azure sets NGINX_RESOLVER to the platform DNS (168.63.129.16), while compose leaves the image default of Docker's embedded 127.0.0.11. nginx resolves the upstream per request rather than once at config load, so an api revision replacing its address does not leave the proxy pointing at nothing — which is why a resolver has to be named at all.

API_DATABASE_URL and API_DATABASE_MIGRATION_URL are set in BOTH environments with different VALUES and identical NAMES, so they are sameEverywhere — exactly like the identity keys in row 1 — and they moved out of this row when Task 24's infra/modules/postgres.bicep and the api Container App's two secretRef entries landed. API_DATABASE_POOL_MAX is defaultedInBothEnvironments: apps/api/src/config.ts falls back to 10 and neither environment sets it. What exists in only one environment is the Postgres container's own bootstrap. Locally the database is a container this stack runs and these three variables are consumed by the postgres image itself at first boot (docker-entrypoint-initdb.d); in a tenant it is a Flexible Server somebody provisioned, whose admin credential comes from a Key Vault secret read with getSecret(), never through a container-image bootstrap variable. The two roles P10 requires — lexprompt_migrator and lexprompt_app — are created by infra/postgres/init.sql locally and by ONE psql run by the Flexible Server admin in Azure; 000_preconditions.sql refuses the migration, naming that step, when they are absent, rather than letting a GRANT fail with 'role does not exist'. One thing that is NOT a divergence and is worth saying so: max_connections is declared explicitly in BOTH — docker-compose.yml's `command:` and postgres.bicep's configuration child resource — rather than inherited from an image default in one and a SKU default in the other, because three of this project's defects have been an undeclared cap.

rowsWithNoKeys.7: Infrastructure, not application code: compose networks versus Container Apps egress rules. Asserted by apps/api/test/egress.compose.test.ts (Task 24) and, in Azure, by Spike 2 — which has not been done, and which the README says plainly is not done.
rowsWithNoKeys.8: The gateway writes the same JSON lines to stdout in both environments (§10.5). What differs is the collector that reads them; no application key varies. Ruling L1 records why there is no log-sink configuration at all to diverge.

sameEverywhereNote: GATEWAY_ALLOWED_JURISDICTIONS is in this list, not in a divergence row,
and that is deliberate and load-bearing. It is not a value that differs
BECAUSE one environment is local; it is a value the operator supplies in
BOTH, from the same source — their own contracts and data provisions —
and neither has a default (P4). Filing it as a divergence would say the
two environments are entitled to different policies, which is the
opposite of what the owner decided. §5.1's own nine-row table does not
defaultedNote: Read by a configuration module, set by NEITHER environment: each falls
back to a value in the module that reads it — the four API_ keys in
apps/api/src/config.ts, the GATEWAY_ ones in apps/gateway/src/config.ts.
They are listed because a key that reaches only one environment's file
stops being a shared default and becomes an undeclared divergence, and
the check that it is set in neither is what catches that the day it
happens rather than on a first deployment.
They are NOT the same case as GATEWAY_ALLOWED_JURISDICTIONS. Each of
these is a property of the software's own behaviour — a size cap, a
timeout, a rate — that the software is entitled to have an opinion
about. Which jurisdictions a firm permits is a property of that firm's
contracts, which the software has no standing to guess at all.

Stage 3 Task 8-12 added thirteen: the run queue's caps (workers, lease, cell timeout, heartbeat, attempts, poll, per-workspace concurrency, parse workers), the outbox's retention and page size, the page-image LRU and the per-call image budget, and the engine pool's size. Every one is a property of the software's own behaviour and every one is DECLARED rather than inherited from a library default -- which is the rule three shipped defects on the scanned-document path bought. API_RUN_IMAGE_BYTES_MAX is the one whose default is DERIVED (three quarters of API_MAX_BODY_BYTES) rather than a constant, so an operator who lowers the body limit does not have to know about a second key to keep the two consistent.

Stage 4 Task 16 added four: the live socket's ping interval, its per-replica connection ceiling, its per-socket subscription ceiling and its maximum client frame size. Every one is a property of the software's own behaviour, defaulted in apps/api/src/config.ts (WS_CAP_DEFAULTS) and set by NEITHER environment -- so they belong here rather than in sameEverywhere, which would require both docker-compose.yml and containerApps.bicep to name them. API_WS_PING_MS is the one with a relationship OUTSIDE this file: it must stay below infra/nginx/web.conf's proxy_read_timeout on the socket location and below Container Apps' ingress idle timeout, or every idle socket dies and the app looks like a network with a fault. That relationship is asserted in wsProxy.compose.test.ts rather than left to a reader comparing two files.

Stage 4 Task 18 added API_HUB_TICK_MS: how often each replica reads the outbox forward for the subscriptions it holds, whether or not a pg_notify arrived. It is the FLOOR live change degrades to when the LISTEN connection has dropped -- a failure whose only symptom is the app feeling one tick slow, which nobody reports -- so the number is declared rather than picked, and defaulted in the module that reads it like every other cap here.

Stage 5 Task 1 added API_ASSIGNMENT_INBOX_LIMIT: how many open requests the cross-matter "assigned to me" inbox reads at once. It is defaultedInBothEnvironments and NOT sameEverywhere -- the task brief said sameEverywhere, and configSurface.test.ts settles it: a sameEverywhere key must be SET in docker-compose.yml AND in containerApps.bicep, and this one is set by neither and falls back in apps/api/src/config.ts like every other cap here. It is read with a limit + 1 so the answer says capped rather than returning a short page, because a counter that renders a number it silently truncated is worse than one that says 200+.

Stage 5 Task 4 added API_SEARCH_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE: how many hits ONE arm of the firm-wide search may return. Per SOURCE and not overall, because the answer reports each source separately -- an overall cap would silently starve whichever arm finished last, with nothing on screen saying which, and "some results are missing" that nobody is told is the defect this whole route is organised against. Same classification and same reasoning as API_ASSIGNMENT_INBOX_LIMIT above.

Stage 4 Task 22 added two: the presence heartbeat interval and the TTL that expires a roster entry. Both are properties of the software's own behaviour, defaulted in apps/api/src/config.ts (WS_CAP_DEFAULTS) and set by NEITHER environment. The heartbeat is the interval the SERVER asks the browser for -- it travels on the hello frame -- rather than a constant compiled into the bundle, so raising it in a deployment cannot leave a browser beating on the old one and expiring between beats. loadConfig refuses a TTL below one and a half heartbeats (assertPresenceOutlivesBeat) for the same reason: the failure it prevents is every colleague flickering on and off a roster, which nobody reports as a fault and which costs the whole feature.
awaitingAzureTemplateEmptyNote: EMPTY, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THE LIST RATHER THAN A REASON TO DELETE
IT. It held exactly one key — API_BLOB_ACCOUNT_URL — from Task 10, when
apps/api could already be pointed at a managed-identity blob store and no
Azure template set the account URL it would need. Task 24 set it, so the
key moved into row 5 and this list emptied, which is what the note below
said would happen. The list stays because the NEXT key of this kind will
arrive the same way: read by a config module, required by one
environment's posture, with no default and no fallback, and set by
neither environment yet. Filing such a key as 'defaulted' would say the
software has an opinion it must not have; leaving it unclassified would
fail the suite with no honest place to put it.
awaitingAzureTemplateNote: Read by a configuration module and set by NEITHER environment — but NOT
the same case as defaultedInBothEnvironments above, which is why it is a
list of its own rather than a line added to that one. Those keys fall
back to a value in a config module and are supposed to be unset. This one
has no default and no fallback: it is REQUIRED whenever
API_BLOB_CREDENTIAL_SOURCE is managed-identity, which is the Azure
posture, and the Azure template that sets it is Task 25's work. Filing it
as 'defaulted' would say the software has an opinion about which storage
account holds a firm's documents, which it must not.
The day containerApps.bicep sets it, this list empties and the key joins
row 5. An entry that outlives that is a key nobody is going to configure,
which is why the check below asserts each one is genuinely set nowhere
